### 4.2.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The doctrine of error (*dwaling*) within the continental Civil Law tradition—rooted in the *error* concept of Roman law—has historically hinged on a single fundamental premise: the autonomy of a rational human will. For centuries, jurists from natural‑law schools to modern codifications such as the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek, BW) have treated mistake as an internal psychological anomaly. Mistake is regarded as a defect that originates within the legal subject itself; a party may misunderstand the object of a contract, misidentify the negotiating counterpart, or misappraise the intrinsic value of a thing because of personal reasoning limitations or a lack of due diligence (*dualisme culpa in contrahendo*). In this classical landscape, Civil Law draws a sharp line between remediable mistake (*verschoonbare dwaling*) and non‑remediable mistake (*onverschoonbare dwaling*), placing the burden of cognitive proof on the errant individual. The epistemology of the past assumed that the objective reality of a transaction could always be accessed by a legal subject employing the *reasonable person standard*.

When we enter the transactional era driven by generative artificial intelligence and Large Language Models (LLMs), this epistemic foundation undergoes a structural collapse. Contractual reality is no longer presented as a static, neutral showcase; it is reconstructed *in real‑time* by personalized latent algorithmic spaces designed to penetrate the subconscious cognitive defenses of humans. Contemporary cognitive error is not the product of passive ignorance but the result of an actively engineered fabrication through algorithmic *framing*. We are confronting a form of structural disinformation masquerading as mathematical objectivity. Recommendation systems and dialogic agents do not merely sell products; they assemble a parallel reality that is emotionally coherent yet substantively deceptive. Consequently, the legal subject is not experiencing an autonomous mistake but is systematically guided into a labyrinth of cognitive distortion where the boundary between free will and programmed persuasion dissolves without any visible trace.

This dynamic compels us to reconceptualize the philosophical meaning of “substantial truth” within a consensus. If traditional *dwaling* doctrine required congruence between external will and internal will (*wilsontbreken*), then in today’s digital ecosystem the internal will itself has been commodified and engineered by computer code. The closest analogy is a wax mask that appears warm and alive under a theatrical spotlight, while its substance is cold, rigid paraffin. Likewise, the information displayed by an AI interface seems responsive, intuitive, and as if it understands the depth of the user’s soul, yet it is merely a statistical projection of token probabilities optimized to trigger transactional conversion. When a party makes a contractual decision based on this machine‑crafted pseudo‑reality, blaming the victim entirely is as unjust as accusing a wanderer lost in a deliberately thick fog released by the opposing party to mislead the compass.

Therefore, the epistemological dimension of *dwaling* must shift from a subjective‑individual orientation to a relational‑structural one. Civil Law can no longer be satisfied merely by asking whether the legal subject misapprehended the substantive nature of the purchased item (*egenschap der zaak*); it must examine how the informational ecosystem surrounding the transaction is constructed. Was the information designed to illuminate or to obscure? Had the algorithmic *framing* employed crossed the threshold of reasonable influence (*undue influence*) and entered the realm of systematic cognitive manipulation? These questions mark a paradigm shift from nineteenth‑century jurisprudence naïve to technological power toward a twenty‑first‑century critical jurisprudence that recognises human cognition as a geopolitical data battlefield where individual cognitive liberty is being wagered on a massive scale.
